name: gorefactor-nil-rules
origin: gorefactor 20629f3 (lint: add unnecessary-nil-check rule, widen redundant-nil-guard)
summary: gorefactor gains a second nil-analysis lint rule and widens the first. `unnecessary-nil-check` walks each function with go/parser and no type information, carrying per-scope facts about which values were constructed non-nil or already guarded, and reports checks it believes cannot fire. `redundant-nil-guard` grows a prologue scan that tolerates earlier guards and caller-side proofs that accept `||` chains and `&&` conjuncts. 9 files, 1329 insertions.
why_this_fixture_exists:
This change modifies existing code rather than adding files, so the context provider carries callers, siblings and history the diff does not contain: 31 of 118 expansions survive deduplication, 26.3% informative, against 4.8% for gorefactor-changectx. That is why it was chosen.

It is also a change whose defects are unusually checkable. A false positive from either rule is advice to delete a nil guard, so following it introduces a nil dereference, and every label was reproduced by building gorefactor at 20629f3 and running the rule on a constructed snippet rather than argued from reading.

CORRECTION. This fixture was originally described as the one a context arm could be run on. That was wrong, and the first context arm run against it (2/12 with context, 4/12 without) does not mean what it appears to. Every one of the first twelve labels is findable from the diff alone: none names an unchanged file, because all twelve were authored by reading the changed files. A label set built that way cannot reward a reviewer for reading beyond the diff; it can only charge one for the tokens spent. Supplying more novel context does not fix that, because the demand was zero.

The two labels keyed `needs-unchanged-file` are the beginning of the class that was missing. Their decisive evidence is in files this commit never touches, so a diff-only reviewer cannot reach them, and a with/without-context comparison scored on them measures what context is for. Two is not enough to run that comparison on; the honest state is that the instrument is still being built. Note what the search cost: two independent readings of the whole repository produced five candidates of this class and only these two survived verification.

expect.what: checkExpr walks an expression with ast.Inspect, which descends into a function literal's body, and the statement walk has no *ast.FuncLit case, so a closure's own parameters never enter the fact map. A nil check on a closure parameter is therefore resolved against the enclosing function's variable of the same name and reported as impossible. Reproduced: an outer `p := &T{N: 1}` beside `func(p *T) { if p == nil { return 0 } }` yields "`p == nil` (line 10) can never be true — p was assigned a non-nil value at line 8". Following the advice removes a mandatory guard on a value the closure's caller controls. Two independent readings anchored this at cmd_lint_unnecessary_nil_check_facts.go:176 and cmd_lint_unnecessary_nil_check.go:278, so no file is required here.

walkIf calls s.checkExpr(st.Cond, scope) and only then invalidateNilFacts(st.Cond, scope), so a finding is emitted before the facts that the condition itself destroys are dropped. Go evaluates && left to right, so a mutating call in the left conjunct really does run before the nil compare in the right one. Reproduced end to end: for `if x.Take() > 0 && x == nil` where Take does `*s = nil`, the rule reports "`x == nil` (line 15) can never be true", and running the same code prints `cond: true`. The tool's claim is falsified by executing the program. The identical ordering exists for AssignStmt right-hand sides.

hasEntryNilGuard's prologue scan gained `case *ast.AssignStmt, *ast.DeclStmt, *ast.ExprStmt: continue`, so it walks past writes to the very parameter it is deciding about. The rule's premise is that the guarded value is the caller's argument, which stops holding once the prologue rebinds it. Reproduced: `func use(a, b *T) { if a == nil { return }; b = normalize(b); if b == nil { return } }` with a single caller `use(&T{N: 1}, &T{N: 2})` reports b's guard as redundant, though it exists to catch normalize returning nil. Before this commit the first `if` decided and the guard was unreachable.

The message reports fn.fset.Position(fn.decl.Pos()).Line as "at entry (line %d)". Now that a prologue may be arbitrarily long, that line names the func keyword rather than the guard the reader is being told to delete, and two findings about two different guards quote the same line. Reproduced: guards on lines 13 and 17 were both reported as "at entry (line 12)", which is the `func use(a, b *T) int {` line.

nilRejectGuardNames treats `if a == nil || b == nil { return }` as a guard for each name, and hasEntryNilGuard returns true for whichever parameter is being considered, but the advice is per-guard: "drop the guard". When callers prove a and not b, only a is reported, and the only guard the reader can drop also removes b's check. The file's own comment eighteen lines below makes exactly this argument for rejecting mixed conditions — "a mixed guard does more than nil-check, so 'drop the guard' is not safe advice for it" — and applies it only to non-nil-compare disjuncts. Reproduced: with `combined(&T{N: 1}, b)` passing an unproven b, only a is reported.

precedingNilReject accepts an earlier sibling `if x == nil { return }` as proof that the argument at a later call is non-nil, and nothing examines what happens to the name between the guard and the call. Reproduced: `if t == nil { return 0 }; t = shrink(t); return guarded(t)` reports guarded's own guard as redundant, though shrink can return nil. enclosingNonNilGuard has the same hole. The flow-insensitivity predates the commit, but both call sites are rewritten here and the widening strictly increases how many sites reach them.
any_of: between the guard and the call

expect.what: The `case *ast.UnaryExpr: if st.Op == token.AND` branch of invalidateNilFacts can only ever rewrite factNone to factNone. closureTaintedNames applies the identical predicate over the whole function body before the walk starts, and every producer of a fact refuses tainted names, so any name this branch could clear is already permanently tainted. The function's own doc comment enumerates assignment targets, redeclarations, range variables and method receivers, and does not mention address-taking, which is consistent with the branch being vestigial. Low severity: dead defensive logic that implies address-taking is handled flow-sensitively when it is handled by whole-function taint.

TestUnnecessaryNilCheck_QuietOnGlobal credits its silence to an intervening call that may reassign a package-level variable, but establishFacts skips any name that is absent from vars or not local, and globals are never entered into vars at all. Reproduced: two identical `if g == nil` checks on a package-level var with no intervening call are silent, while the same shape on a local is reported. Delete the mutate() call, or every invalidateNilFacts call site, and the test still passes.

hasGotoOrLabel returns true on the first *ast.LabeledStmt, and Go requires a goto's target label in the same function, so the BranchStmt/token.GOTO arm can never be the deciding factor for any valid input: TestUnnecessaryNilCheck_SkipsGotoFunctions stays green with that arm deleted. The consequence beyond the test is larger — the predicate disables the rule for every function containing a label with no goto, such as a labelled for with `break outer` — and no test distinguishes the two reasons for skipping.

Every test routes through wantIssueCount, which asserts len(issues) and iss.Rule and nothing else; neither test file contains a single reference to the issue's File. The rule builds its location as fmt.Sprintf("%s:%d", s.file, s.line(be)), and this release's changelog headlines exactly that: findings now carry their line as path:line so consumers can point at the finding in code. A bug emitting a bare path, the enclosing FuncDecl's position, or the wrong file when several are linted would pass the whole suite.

The changelog and README advertise slice and map literals as construction facts, and the constructed-value test covers only `&T{N: 1}`, `new(T)` and `make(map[string]int)`. No fixture in either test file assigns a slice or map composite literal, so the *ast.CompositeLit branch of constructedNonNil is dead as far as the suite is concerned. Returning no fact for composite literals, or treating an array literal as a nilable slice, would ship green against a documented claim.

The widening's headline caller-side proof accepts `x != nil && ...`, and the guard rule's fixtures contain no caller-side `!= nil` guard at all: every one proves non-nil by construction or by a preceding `x == nil` reject. enclosingNonNilGuard and the multi-conjunct tolerance of nonNilConjunctNames are never executed by the suite. Both failure directions are invisible — a proof that never matches silently halves the widening, and one that matches too loosely tells users to delete a load-bearing nil guard.

The rule's len-combo facet reports `x != nil && len(x) > 0`, which is exactly staticcheck's S1009. The repository already enables staticcheck in .golangci.yml -- a file this commit does not touch -- and that same file states the policy this breaks in its own comments: "cyclop/funlen/dupl are intentionally NOT enabled: gorefactor owns the size/shape sensors and their autofixes. Running both double-counts the same defects in doctor --report." cmd_lint_golangci.go turns each golangci finding into its own lintIssue, and doctor/score.go exempts neither rule, so one line yields two findings at full weight in the merged report and the health score. Reproduced: on `if xs != nil && len(xs) > 0`, gorefactor at this revision says "`xs != nil` (line 4) is redundant -- len(nil) == 0" and staticcheck says "S1009: should omit nil check". Both scouts that read the repository found this independently. A reviewer with only the nine changed files cannot reach it: the new rule is unobjectionable in isolation and wrong only against an unchanged config file and the policy written in it.

The widening exists to prove a callee's entry guard redundant from its call sites, but argProvenNonNil takes `id, ok := arg.(*ast.Ident); if !ok { return false }`, so any argument that is not a bare identifier is rejected before the new proofs run. In this repository the real guarded helpers are called with selector expressions: analyzer/cross_file_helpers.go:107 `func countStatements(block *ast.BlockStmt) int { if block == nil { return 0 } }` is called at analyzer/cross_file_analyzer.go:157 as `countStatements(fn.Body)`, and the same shape holds for parser/parser.go:184 parseFieldList, orchestrator/op_helpers.go:109 extractOldName and refactor/changesig/calls.go:184 interfaceConflicts. None of those files is in this commit. Confirmed by running the rules over the whole tree at this revision: both fire zero times on 4,758 nodes, so 1,329 added lines change no output here. The diff shows the proofs getting wider and cannot show that every argument they would meet is a selector.
